description.en: The alternate heel touch side kick squat is a dynamic conditioning move that pairs squats with heel touches and side kicks. The lifter squats, touches a heel, then performs a side kick before alternating sides. It builds leg endurance and obliques.

en: Stand with the feet wider than shoulder width.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Squat down and touch one heel with the opposite hand.
Stand back up.
Kick the same leg out to the side at hip height.
Lower the leg back down.
Squat again and repeat with the other side.
Continue alternating sides.
Burns calories
Trains the legs
Builds the obliques
Strong conditioning move
Useful for cardio
No equipment needed

description.en: The backward abdominal stretch is a standing backbend that lengthens the abs and hip flexors while improving spinal extension. Standing tall with hands on the lower back, you arch backward through the upper spine. The stretch counteracts forward-flexed postures and improves spinal mobility.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Place your hands on your lower back for support.
Brace your core slightly to protect the lower back.
Pull your shoulders back and lift your chest.
Slowly arch backward through the upper spine.
Lead the bend with the chest, not the lower back.
Continue until you feel a stretch in the abs and front of the body.
Hold the stretch briefly, then return to upright.
Opens the abs and hip flexors
Improves spinal extension
Counteracts forward-flexed posture
No equipment required
Useful for desk workers
Easy to do anywhere

description.en: The band alternate low row with twist combines a low rowing pull with a torso rotation. The alternating pull and rotation strengthens the lats, mid back, and obliques for athletic rotational power.

en: Anchor a resistance band at low height and grasp a handle in each hand.
Step back to create tension and stand with knees slightly bent.
Hinge slightly forward at the hips with a tall back.
Pull one handle back toward the hip while rotating the torso.
Squeeze the back of the shoulder and keep the elbow tucked.
Return the arm forward and untwist back to center.
Repeat the row and twist with the opposite arm.
Continue alternating sides for the desired number of reps.
Builds the lats, rhomboids, and rear deltoids unilaterally.
Trains the obliques through controlled rotation.
Improves anti rotation control as the opposite side stabilizes.
Joint friendly resistance from the band.
Carryover to athletic rotational pulling movements.
Adds rotational variety to standard rowing patterns.

description.en: The barbell incline lying rear delt raise is a strict rear delt exercise performed face down on an incline bench. Holding a barbell with a wide grip, you raise the bar in a Y-pattern up and away from the body. The chest support eliminates body english and forces strict rear delt isolation.

en: Set a bench to about a 30 degree incline.
Lie face down (chest on the bench) with a light barbell on the floor.
Reach down and grip the bar with hands wider than shoulder-width.
Hold the bar with palms facing down (overhand grip).
Maintain a slight bend in the elbows.
Brace your core and squeeze your shoulder blades together.
Raise the bar up and away from your body in a Y-shape.
Squeeze the rear delts at the top, then lower with control.
Strict rear delt isolation
Chest support eliminates body english
Builds rear delt and upper back size
Strong rhomboid engagement
Different stimulus than dumbbell raises
Useful for shoulder specialization

description.en: The barbell pause decline bench press combines the lower-chest emphasis of the decline bench with a deliberate pause at the chest. The pause kills any rebound from the chest, forcing the pecs and triceps to handle a true dead start out of the bottom. It builds raw concentric strength in the lower pec.

en: Set up a decline bench and load the barbell.
Lie back with feet secured on the foot pads, eyes under the bar.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Unrack the bar and hold it over your lower chest with arms extended.
Lower the bar with control until it touches your lower chest.
Pause for a full second at the chest, holding tension.
Drive the bar back up by pressing through the chest and triceps.
Lock out at the top, then lower for the next rep with the same pause.
Builds lower chest strength from a dead start
Eliminates the stretch reflex and bouncing
Develops raw concentric pressing power
Improves bar control under heavy loads
Strong carryover to competitive bench press
Reveals weak points at the chest position

description.en: The bodyweight full squat with overhead press performs a deep squat followed by reaching the arms overhead at the top, mimicking an overhead press without weight. It is a useful warm-up, mobility drill, and bodyweight conditioning move that trains the legs and shoulders together.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and arms at your sides.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Squat down by sitting your hips back and bending the knees.
Continue until your thighs are below parallel to the floor.
Drive up through your heels to standing.
As you stand tall, press your arms straight overhead.
Lock out the arms with hands above your head.
Lower the arms back to your sides as you start the next squat.
Trains legs and shoulders together
Useful as a warm-up
Improves squat depth and shoulder mobility
No equipment required
Time-efficient combo move
Good for conditioning

description.en: The bodyweight kneeling hold to stand is a balance and strength drill that takes you from a kneeling hold up to standing. The transition builds single leg drive and total body coordination.

en: Begin in a tall kneeling position with both knees on the floor.
Brace the core and keep the chest tall.
Step one foot forward into a half kneeling position.
Drive through the front heel to stand up to a tall stance.
Stand fully tall with both feet under the hips.
Step the same foot back and lower into the half kneeling position.
Lower the back knee to return to the tall kneeling start.
Repeat on the same side then switch.
Builds single leg strength through the rise.
Improves balance and coordination.
No equipment needed.
Trains hip mobility and quad strength.
Functional carryover to daily life.
Excellent rehab and prehab move.

description.en: The bodyweight kneeling triceps extension is a kneeling skullcrusher style move with bodyweight. The lifter kneels in front of a bench and lowers the forehead toward the bench by bending the elbows. The bodyweight load builds the triceps without weights.

en: Kneel on a pad in front of a sturdy bench.
Place the hands on the edge of the bench at shoulder width.
Walk the knees back so the body forms a straight diagonal line.
Set the upper arms parallel to the floor.
Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line.
Lower the body by bending the elbows toward the bench.
Stop just before the forehead touches the bench.
Press back up to extension by extending the elbows.
Bodyweight tricep builder
No equipment beyond a bench
Trains the long head
Strong tricep move
Useful for travel
Builds the chest

description.en: The bodyweight swing performs the kettlebell swing motion with no weight — clasped hands swing between the legs and up to chest height using explosive hip drive. It teaches the swing pattern before loading with a kettlebell.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Clasp hands together in front of you.
Hinge at the hips. Swing your clasped hands between your legs.
Drive your hips forward explosively.
Your arms swing up to chest or eye height from the hip drive.
Let your arms swing back between your legs as you hinge again.
Continue the swing-hinge rhythm.
The power comes from the hips — not the arms.
Aim for 15 to 25 reps as a drill or warm-up.
Teaches the swing hip drive pattern
No equipment needed
Warm-up before loaded swings
Develops hip hinge explosiveness
Builds posterior chain awareness
Accessible for beginners

description.en: The cable front shoulder raise is a front deltoid isolation exercise using a low cable pulley. It is functionally identical to the cable front raise and cable forward raise — all target the anterior deltoid by raising the arm forward to shoulder height against cable resistance.

en: Set a cable to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle or straight bar.
Face away from the cable. Grip the handle between your legs or at your side.
Stand tall. Brace your core.
Raise the handle forward to shoulder height with a straight arm.
Squeeze your front delt at the top.
Lower under control.
Maintain slight elbow bend.
Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Constant cable tension for front delt isolation
Tension even at the bottom of the raise
Easy to load progressively
Strict isolation
Joint-friendly
Different resistance curve than dumbbells

description.en: The cable hip adduction uses a low cable with an ankle strap to pull one leg across the body, targeting the adductors (inner thigh muscles). It provides constant cable tension through the adduction range and is easy to load progressively.

en: Attach an ankle strap to a low cable. Strap it around your right ankle.
Stand sideways to the cable with the working leg closest to the cable.
Hold the frame for balance.
Pull your right leg across your body to the left against the cable tension.
Continue until your right leg crosses past your left.
Squeeze your inner thigh at the end position.
Slowly return to start.
Complete reps, then switch legs. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Isolates the adductors with constant cable tension
Easy to load progressively
Helps prevent groin strains
Builds hip strength balance
Adjustable cable resistance
Useful for athletic training

description.en: The cable one arm high pulley overhead tricep extension uses a high pulley setup. With the body facing away from the cable, you press one hand from behind the head up overhead to bias the triceps long head.

en: Set a cable pulley to the highest setting and attach a single handle.
Face away from the cable and grab the handle with one hand.
Step forward and bring the elbow up next to the head.
Plant the feet in a split stance for stability.
Brace the core and keep the elbow pointing forward.
Extend the elbow by pressing the hand up overhead.
Squeeze the triceps at the top.
Lower with control and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Biases the triceps long head through overhead position.
Cable provides constant tension throughout.
Trains one arm at a time for symmetry.
Carryover to pressing strength.
Easy to scale by adjusting cable weight.
Develops triceps size and lockout strength.

description.en: The cable one arm incline fly on exercise ball is a unilateral upper chest fly. Bridged on a stability ball with the upper back as the incline, the cable provides constant tension while the fly isolates one side of the upper pec.

en: Set a cable handle at low height.
Sit on a stability ball with feet flat on the floor.
Walk the feet out and bridge the upper back onto the ball.
Grab the handle with one arm extended out to the side.
Brace the core and keep the hips lifted.
Pull the handle up and across the body in a fly arc.
Squeeze the chest at the top centerline.
Return with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Isolates the upper chest.
Cable provides constant tension.
Ball adds core challenge.
Useful chest accessory.
Builds upper pec.

description.en: The cable squatting curl combines a bicep curl with a sustained squat hold. You stand at a low cable, squat to a half or full squat position, and perform bicep curls while maintaining the squat. It builds bicep strength and quad endurance simultaneously.

en: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a straight bar or EZ bar handle.
Face the cable. Grip the handle with an underhand grip.
Squat down to a half or parallel squat position. Hold this position throughout.
Curl the handle up toward your shoulders by bending at the elbows.
Squeeze your biceps at the top.
Lower under control. Continue curling while maintaining the squat.
Complete your curls, then stand up.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 curls per set.
Combines bicep curls with leg endurance
Time-efficient — trains arms and legs
Squat hold builds quad endurance
Constant cable tension on curls
Engaging and challenging variation
Builds mental toughness

description.en: The cable standing close grip row is performed standing at a low cable pulley with a v-handle attachment. Pulling the handle to your stomach with elbows tucked tight builds lat thickness while the standing position adds core engagement to maintain posture. It is a strong choice for back development.

en: Set a cable to a low pulley with a v-handle attachment.
Stand facing the cable with feet hip-width apart.
Grip the handle with both hands, palms facing each other.
Step back to create cable tension and lean forward slightly.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Pull the handle to your stomach by driving the elbows back along your sides.
Squeeze the lats and rhomboids at the back of the row.
Slowly extend the arms forward to the starting position with control.
Builds back thickness
Standing position adds core engagement
Constant cable tension
Strong lat involvement
Different angle than seated row
Useful for back training

description.en: The crossed arms front leg kick is a dynamic warm up drill that kicks the legs forward while the arms cross over the chest. The combination challenges balance and opens the hamstrings.

en: Stand tall with feet hip width apart and arms crossed over the chest.
Brace the core and keep the chest tall.
Lift one straight leg forward and up to about hip height.
Aim to keep the leg straight without losing posture.
Lower the leg back to the floor with control.
Repeat with the opposite leg.
Maintain the crossed arms throughout the set.
Continue alternating leg kicks for the full duration.
Stretches the hamstrings dynamically.
Builds balance and single leg control.
Warms up the hips before lifting or sport.
Engages the quads and core.
No equipment needed.
Excellent dynamic warm up move.

description.en: The dumbbell clean and press is a full-body compound lift where you clean a dumbbell from the floor (or hang) to your shoulder, then press it overhead to lockout. The combined movement trains the entire body — legs, back, shoulders, and arms — in a single rep. It is excellent for building total-body strength and conditioning with home-friendly equipment.

en: Place a pair of dumbbells on the floor between your feet. Stand with feet hip-width apart.
Hinge down and grip the dumbbells with palms facing your body. Set your back flat and chest tall.
Brace your core. Drive your feet through the floor and pull the dumbbells up explosively, keeping them close to your body.
As the dumbbells reach hip height, drop your elbows under and “catch” the dumbbells in the front-rack position at shoulder height with palms facing each other.
Stand fully tall with the dumbbells racked at your shoulders. Brace your core hard for the press.
Press both dumbbells straight up overhead until your arms are fully extended.
Lock out at the top with the dumbbells directly above your shoulders.
Lower the dumbbells back to your shoulders, then back down to the floor under control. Reset and repeat for the desired number of reps.
Trains the entire body in one movement
Builds total-body strength and conditioning
Time-efficient combination of multiple lifts
Independent dumbbells expose left-right imbalances
Trains hip extension power and overhead pressing strength
Works at home with one pair of dumbbells

description.en: The dumbbell front plank arm raise is performed in a high plank holding dumbbells while raising one arm forward at a time. The plank position challenges the core, while the front raise hits the front delt. The need to anti-rotate makes the obliques work hard to keep the hips square.

en: Get into a high plank position holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Position your hands directly under your shoulders.
Spread your feet wider than hip-width for stability.
Brace your core and keep your hips square to the floor.
With one arm, raise the dumbbell straight forward to shoulder height.
Keep the elbow with a slight bend.
Lower the dumbbell back to the floor with control.
Switch sides and continue alternating.
Combines plank stability and shoulder work
Trains anti-rotation core control
Builds front deltoid strength
Improves total body coordination
Useful for athletic training
Brutal core engagement

description.en: The dumbbell full can lateral raise is a lateral raise variation with thumbs pointing up (like pouring from a full can) rather than the traditional thumbs-down (empty can). The thumbs-up position is generally considered safer for the supraspinatus and reduces impingement risk.

en: Stand with dumbbells at your sides, thumbs pointing forward (neutral grip).
Raise both dumbbells out to the sides at a slight forward angle (about 30 degrees forward of directly lateral).
Keep your thumbs pointing up throughout the raise.
Lift to shoulder height.
Lower under control.
The thumbs-up position reduces supraspinatus impingement risk.
Use light weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Move with controlled tempo.
Safer for the shoulder joint than empty-can raises
Reduces supraspinatus impingement risk
Still targets the lateral deltoid effectively
Recommended by physical therapists
Easy to load progressively
Builds shoulder size safely

description.en: The dumbbell incline alternate hammer curl combines the stretch of incline curls with a hammer (neutral) grip. The incline angle fully stretches the brachialis and biceps at the bottom while the neutral grip emphasizes the brachialis and brachioradialis for thicker arms.

en: Set an incline bench to about 45 to 60 degrees.
Sit back on the bench with a dumbbell in each hand.
Allow your arms to hang fully extended toward the floor.
Use a neutral grip with palms facing each other (hammer grip).
Pin your shoulders back against the bench.
Curl the right dumbbell up by bending only at the elbow, keeping the hammer grip.
Squeeze the bicep and brachialis at the top, then lower with control.
Repeat with the left arm. Alternate sides each rep.
Strong stretch on the brachialis at the bottom
Hammer grip targets brachialis and brachioradialis
Alternating pattern increases time under tension
Builds arm thickness
Useful for hypertrophy training
Strong forearm engagement

description.en: The dumbbell Kas glute bridge (named after coach Kassem Hanson) is a glute bridge variation that focuses only on the top portion of the range — the part where the glutes are maximally contracted. You perform short-range reps from just below lockout to full extension, keeping constant tension on the glutes.

en: Lie flat on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Place a dumbbell across your hips, just below your hip bones. Hold it in place with both hands.
Brace your core. Drive through your heels and lift your hips to a standard bridge position.
Now lower your hips only halfway down — about 4 to 6 inches below the top.
Drive back up to the full bridge position. Squeeze your glutes hard.
Lower halfway and drive up again. The reps stay in the top half of the range.
Maintain constant glute tension throughout — never relaxing fully at the bottom.
Perform 10 to 15 reps per set.
Maximizes glute contraction by staying in the top range
Constant glute tension throughout the set
Builds glute size and strength effectively
Excellent for glute mind-muscle connection
Works at home with one dumbbell
Reduced lower-back strain vs heavy hip thrusts

description.en: The dumbbell seated alternate overhead triceps extension is a seated overhead extension where one arm works at a time. The alternating pattern allows full focus on each side and a deep stretch on the long head of the triceps. It is a strong overall triceps builder.

en: Sit on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand pressed overhead.
Keep your back tall and core braced.
Pin your upper arms close to your ears.
Lower one dumbbell behind your head by bending the elbow.
Keep the upper arm still and only the elbow moves.
Pause when you feel a deep triceps stretch.
Press the dumbbell back up to overhead lockout.
Switch arms and repeat in alternating fashion.
Targets the long head of triceps
Allows full focus per side
Deep stretch under load
Builds arm size
Single-arm balance work
Excellent for arm day

description.en: The dumbbell single-leg deadlift is a unilateral hip-hinge exercise where you balance on one leg while hinging forward and lowering a dumbbell (or two) toward the floor. It builds the glutes and hamstrings on each side independently while training balance, ankle stability, and core control. It is an excellent accessory for athletic performance and injury prevention.

en: Stand tall on your right leg holding a dumbbell in your left hand (opposite the standing leg). Your left foot rests lightly behind you for balance, but most weight is on the right leg.
Soft-bend your right knee and hold that fixed angle throughout. Brace your core hard.
Begin the descent by hinging forward at the right hip. As you hinge, let your left leg lift behind you to counterbalance.
Keep your hips square — do not let your left hip rotate up. Keep your back flat with a slight natural arch.
Lower the dumbbell along the front of your right leg toward the floor. Continue until your torso and left leg form a straight line roughly parallel to the floor.
Reverse the movement by squeezing your right glute and driving your hips forward to stand back up. The left leg returns to the start position.
Tap the left toe down briefly between reps for balance, or hold it off the floor for more challenge.
Complete all reps on the right leg, then switch and balance on the left leg with the dumbbell in the right hand.
Builds the glutes and hamstrings unilaterally
Trains balance, ankle stability, and core control
Exposes and corrects left-right strength imbalances
Excellent injury-prevention exercise for athletes
Easier on the lower back than barbell deadlifts
Works at home with one dumbbell

description.en: Half Moon Pose (Ardha Chandrasana) is an intermediate yoga balancing pose where you stand on one leg with your torso parallel to the floor, the opposite leg lifted parallel to the floor, and one arm reaching toward the ceiling. It builds balance, core strength, and lateral flexibility.

en: Start in Triangle Pose with right leg forward, left arm reaching up.
Bend your right knee slightly. Slide your left hand up your left thigh.
Place your right hand on the floor (or a block) about 12 inches in front of and outside your right foot.
Shift your weight onto your right leg. Lift your left leg parallel to the floor.
Straighten your right leg. Stack your left hip directly over your right hip.
Reach your left arm toward the ceiling. Stack your left shoulder over your right.
Gaze up at your top hand or straight ahead for balance.
Hold for 5 to 8 breaths. To exit, bend the standing knee and release back into Triangle.
Builds single-leg balance and ankle stability
Strengthens the standing-leg glute and core
Improves lateral flexibility and hip mobility
Opens the chest and shoulders
Develops focus and body awareness
Intermediate yoga balance pose

description.en: The hands release push-up lowers the chest fully to the floor and briefly lifts the hands off the ground before driving back up. The hand release at the bottom eliminates any momentum or bounce and forces a true full range of motion. It is the standard for military fitness tests.

en: Get into a push-up position with hands under shoulders.
Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line.
Bend your elbows to lower your entire chest to the floor.
Pause briefly with your chest fully on the ground.
Lift your hands off the floor briefly.
Place your hands back down under your shoulders.
Press through your hands to drive back up.
Lock out the elbows at the top.
Eliminates bounce or momentum
Forces full range of motion
Standard military fitness move
Builds true pressing strength
No equipment required
Excellent push-up progression

description.en: The handboard open hand grip is a finger and forearm builder used by climbers. The lifter hangs from a hangboard or finger board using an open hand grip. It builds grip endurance and finger strength.

en: Set up a hangboard at a doorway or wall.
Reach up and grip the holds with an open hand grip.
Keep the fingers straight rather than crimped.
Brace your core and keep the shoulders engaged.
Hang from the holds with feet off the floor.
Hold the hang with arms slightly bent.
Lower the feet to the floor when needed.
Continue for the working set.
Builds finger strength
Trains the forearms
Useful for climbing
Strong grip drill
Builds grip endurance

description.en: High knee skips are a classic running drill where you skip forward (or in place) while driving each knee up high with the skip. They build sprint mechanics, hip flexor power, calf elasticity, and cardiovascular conditioning. They are a staple drill in track and field warm-ups.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Pump your arms naturally bent at 90 degrees.
Hop forward (or in place) on your left foot while driving your right knee up high toward your chest.
Land back on your right foot. Hop on your right foot while driving your left knee up high.
Continue alternating in a skipping rhythm.
Pump your arms in opposition to the legs — left arm forward when right knee rises.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Aim for height in both the knee drive and the hop.
If moving forward, take small forward steps with each skip.
Perform for 20 to 45 seconds per set or for distance.
Builds sprint mechanics and hip flexor power
Develops calf elasticity
Excellent cardiovascular conditioning
Standard track and field warm-up drill
Improves coordination and rhythm
No equipment needed

description.en: The incline reverse hyperextension is performed lying face down on an incline bench with the legs hanging off the lower end. The legs lift up and back, hyperextending the hips. The incline angle increases the range of motion compared to a flat bench. It builds the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back.

en: Set an incline bench at about a 30 to 45 degree angle.
Lie face down on the bench with your hips at the lower edge.
Allow your legs to hang straight down off the bench.
Grip the bench with your hands for stability.
Brace your core and keep your legs straight.
Lift both legs up and back until they are roughly in line with your torso.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top.
Lower slowly to the start.
Builds glute and hamstring strength
Strengthens the lower back
Increased range from incline angle
Spinal-friendly compared to traditional hyper
No equipment beyond a bench
Useful as a posterior chain accessory

description.en: The inverted row slide on floor is an inverted row variation that uses sliders or towels under the heels. The legs slide forward as the lifter rows up, adding a hamstring component. It builds back and grip strength using just bodyweight tools.

en: Set up under a low bar with sliders under the heels.
Grip the bar with an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder width.
Set the body in a straight line.
Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades.
Pull the chest toward the bar.
Let the heels slide forward as you pull up.
Squeeze the upper back at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
Builds the back
Trains the biceps
Strong inverted row
Adds hamstring work
Useful bodyweight move
Builds upper back size

description.en: The kettlebell bent arm pullover with knees bent is a chest and lat exercise. Lying flat with knees bent and pulling a kettlebell overhead with bent elbows trains the lats through their full stretch.

en: Lie on your back on a flat bench or the floor.
Bend your knees and place feet flat on the surface.
Hold a kettlebell with both hands by the handle above the chest.
Bend the elbows so the forearms are roughly parallel.
Brace the core and keep the lower back pressed down.
Lower the kettlebell back over your head with bent elbows.
Feel the stretch in the lats and chest at the bottom.
Pull the kettlebell back over the chest by squeezing the lats and repeat.
Hits the lats hard through the overhead stretch.
Builds chest size with the pullover motion.
Strengthens the long head of the triceps.
Improves shoulder mobility through full overhead range.
Bent knees protect the lower back.
Easy to load progressively.

description.en: The kettlebell one-arm swing is a single-arm version of the two-hand swing where you hold the kettlebell with one hand throughout the explosive hip-hinge movement. The asymmetric load adds a significant anti-rotation core challenge and builds unilateral grip strength.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Place the kettlebell between your feet.
Hinge down and grip the handle with one hand, overhand grip.
Hike the bell back between your legs. Set your back flat.
Snap your hips forward explosively. The bell swings up to chest or shoulder height.
Keep your hips and shoulders square — resist the rotation from the one-arm load.
Let the bell swing back between your legs. Hinge at the hips as it passes your knees.
Continue for the desired reps, then switch hands.
You can switch hands at the top of the swing by briefly releasing and catching with the other hand.
Builds unilateral hip power and grip strength
Adds anti-rotation core challenge vs two-hand swing
Develops grip endurance for heavier lifts
Excellent conditioning exercise
Needs only one kettlebell
Progression from the two-hand swing

description.en: The kettlebell single-arm swing is functionally identical to the one-arm swing — an explosive hip-hinge movement holding the kettlebell with one hand. The asymmetric load builds grip endurance and core anti-rotation strength beyond the two-hand version. This is a standard event in kettlebell sport.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, KB on the floor between your feet.
Hinge down and grip with one hand. Hike the bell back between your legs.
Snap your hips forward explosively. Bell swings to chest height.
Keep hips and shoulders square. Resist rotation.
Let the bell swing back. Continue for desired reps, then switch.
Focus on explosive hip drive — the arm guides, it does not lift.
Use moderate weight until grip and anti-rotation are solid.
Breathe: exhale on the hip snap, inhale on the backswing.
Builds unilateral hip power and grip endurance
Anti-rotation core challenge
Standard kettlebell sport event
Excellent conditioning exercise
Develops grip for heavier pulling exercises
Needs only one kettlebell

description.en: The kettlebell sumo deadlift is a wide-stance deadlift variation performed with a kettlebell held between your legs. The wide stance with toes turned out shifts emphasis to the glutes and adductors, while the kettlebell's shape allows it to sit between your feet for a clean pulling line. It is one of the simplest at-home glute-building deadlifts.

en: Place a kettlebell on the floor between your feet.
Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees.
Sit your hips back and down. Reach down and grip the kettlebell handle with both hands.
Brace your core. Lift your chest.
Drive through your full feet to stand up explosively. Squeeze your glutes hard.
Stand fully tall at the top with hips locked out.
Lower the kettlebell under control by hinging at the hips and bending knees.
Touch the kettlebell to the floor between your feet. Repeat for the desired reps.
Targets the glutes and adductors
Easier on the lower back than barbell deadlifts
Easy to set up at home
Builds posterior chain strength
Joint-friendly with one kettlebell
Useful for beginners learning the deadlift pattern

description.en: The lying lat pulldown lies on the floor face up and drives the elbows into the floor to lift the upper back, activating the lats without any equipment. It is a lat activation drill that teaches lat engagement for pull-ups and rows.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat.
Bend your elbows to 90 degrees. Position them at your sides on the floor.
Drive your elbows hard into the floor, pressing down.
This should lift your upper back slightly off the floor using your lats.
Hold the lifted position for 2 to 3 seconds.
Relax and lower.
Focus on squeezing your lats to create the lift.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Teaches lat engagement with zero equipment
Useful for developing pull-up mind-muscle connection
Beginner-friendly lat activation
Can be done anywhere
Develops lat awareness
Useful warm-up before pulling exercises

description.en: The lying scissor kick lies on your back with legs slightly off the floor and alternates kicking them up and down in a scissors pattern. It builds lower ab and hip flexor endurance with sustained tension.

en: Lie on your back. Press your lower back into the floor. Arms at your sides.
Lift both legs 6 to 12 inches off the floor.
Alternately raise one leg up (about 45 degrees) while the other stays low.
Switch in a scissor pattern.
Move with control — not speed.
Keep both legs off the floor throughout.
If your lower back arches, raise legs higher.
Aim for 15 to 25 kicks per leg or work for time.
Builds lower ab and hip flexor endurance
Sustained tension throughout the set
No equipment needed
Simple and accessible
Builds core endurance
Useful finisher exercise

description.en: The lever unilateral row is performed on a chest-supported leverage machine that allows you to row one arm at a time. The chest support eliminates lower back stress and the single-arm pattern lets you focus on each side of the back independently. It builds back size and corrects imbalances.

en: Adjust the leverage row machine seat so the chest pad sits at sternum height.
Sit at the machine with your chest pressed firmly to the pad.
Grip a single handle with your right hand.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Pull the handle back by driving your elbow back toward your hip.
Squeeze your shoulder blade in toward your spine at the back.
Slowly return to the starting position with arm fully extended.
Complete reps on one side, then switch arms.
Chest support eliminates lower back stress
Single-arm pattern corrects imbalances
Builds back size and thickness
Allows progressive heavy loading
Strong lat and rhomboid engagement
Useful for hypertrophy training

description.en: The medicine ball standing overhead throw is a power exercise where you stand and throw a medicine ball forward from an overhead position, using your core, lats, and hip drive to generate maximum velocity. It is similar to a soccer throw-in motion and builds full-body explosive power.

en: Stand with feet staggered (one foot forward, one back) facing a wall or open space.
Hold a medicine ball overhead with both hands, arms extended.
Lean back slightly, loading the throw.
Drive forward by stepping into the throw and whipping the ball forward using your core and lats.
Release the ball at the peak of the throw for maximum distance or velocity.
Follow through with your arms and body.
Retrieve the ball and repeat.
Use maximum effort each throw. Aim for 6 to 10 throws per set.
Builds full-body explosive power
Develops core and lat power
Similar to soccer throw-in — sport-specific
Excellent for athletes
Engaging power exercise
Time-efficient

description.en: The prisoner get-up starts lying on the floor with hands behind your head (prisoner position) and stands up without using your hands. It tests and builds leg strength, hip mobility, and body control. It is a functional fitness assessment and exercise.

en: Lie on your back with hands behind your head, elbows wide.
Without using your hands (they stay behind your head), rise to a standing position.
You may roll to one side, bring one knee up, and step up — whatever works.
Stand fully upright.
Lower yourself back to the floor in a controlled manner without using your hands.
That is one rep.
Aim for 5 to 10 reps per set.
This becomes harder with age and reduced mobility — track your progress.
Functional full-body movement
Tests and builds leg strength and mobility
No equipment needed
Builds body control
Useful fitness assessment
Develops real-world functional strength

description.en: The resistance band clamshell is a glute medius activation exercise where you lie on your side with knees bent and a mini band above your knees, then open your top knee upward against the band like a clamshell opening. It is the gold-standard glute medius activation exercise used in physical therapy and warm-ups.

en: Place a mini band around both thighs just above your knees.
Lie on your right side with knees bent at 90 degrees, feet together.
Keep your feet together throughout.
Open your left (top) knee upward against the band, like a clamshell opening. Keep feet touching.
Open as far as possible. Squeeze your left glute at the top.
Slowly close your knee back to the start.
Complete 15 to 20 reps, then switch sides.
Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Gold-standard glute medius activation
Used in physical therapy worldwide
Builds hip stability and knee tracking
Prevents knee valgus
Highly portable
Excellent warm-up before lower-body training

description.en: The rounded back extension performs a back extension on a GHD or Roman chair with intentional spinal flexion and extension rather than maintaining a flat back. You round your spine at the bottom and extend it at the top, working the erector spinae through spinal flexion and extension range.

en: Set up on a GHD or back extension machine. Face down, hips on the pad.
Lower your torso down. Allow your spine to round at the bottom.
Extend back up by uncurling your spine — segment by segment from bottom to top.
Continue until your torso is in line with your legs or slightly above.
Squeeze your erector spinae at the top.
Lower with control, allowing the spine to round again.
Use bodyweight only. The intentional rounding means this should not be loaded heavily.
Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Works the erector spinae through full flexion-extension range
Builds spinal segmental control
Different stimulus from flat-back extensions
Useful for back endurance
Develops spinal awareness
Bodyweight only for safety

description.en: Side-lying scissors lie on your side and alternately lift the top leg up (abduction) and the bottom leg up (adduction) in a scissor pattern. It works both the hip abductors and adductors in one exercise.

en: Lie on your right side with legs extended and stacked.
Support your head with your right hand.
Lift your top (left) leg up. As you lower it, lift your bottom (right) leg up.
Continue alternating in a scissor pattern.
The top leg works the abductors; the bottom leg works the adductors.
Move with control.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Aim for 15 to 20 scissors per side.
Works both hip abductors and adductors
No equipment needed
Engaging side-lying exercise
Builds hip stability
Useful warm-up or rehab
Develops coordination

description.en: The side plank bent leg lift is a side plank variation that adds a top leg lift. The lifter holds a side plank with the bottom knee bent for support and lifts the top leg. It combines oblique and glute medius work.

en: Lie on the side with the bottom forearm on the floor.
Bend the bottom knee for support.
Stack the hips and shoulders.
Brace your core and lift the hips into a side plank.
Extend the top leg straight.
Lift the top leg up toward the ceiling.
Squeeze the glute medius at the top.
Lower with control. Finish then switch sides.
Loads the obliques
Trains the glute medius
Strong side plank variation
Useful for athletes
Builds the core

description.en: The sideway leg bridge is a side glute bridge variation that combines a side plank with a top leg lift. The lifter lies on the side, presses up into a side plank, and lifts the top leg high. The combo loads the glute medius and obliques hard.

en: Lie on your side with the legs stacked.
Set the bottom forearm on the floor under the shoulder.
Stack the feet and press up into a side plank.
Set the body in a straight line.
Brace your core and squeeze the glutes.
Lift the top leg high while holding the side plank.
Hold the elevated position briefly.
Lower the leg with control. Drop down then switch sides.
Strong glute medius builder
Trains the obliques
Combo side plank move
No equipment needed
Useful for athletes
Strong hip stability move

description.en: The Smith machine incline bench press is a guided pressing exercise performed on an incline bench positioned under a Smith machine bar. The fixed bar path removes stabilizer demand and allows you to focus purely on pressing the upper chest to failure with added safety from the lockout hooks.

en: Position an adjustable bench at 30 to 45 degrees inside a Smith machine so the bar tracks over your upper chest.
Lie back with your eyes directly under the bar. Plant both feet firmly on the floor.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Wrap your thumbs around the bar.
Pull your shoulder blades down and back into the bench. Lift your chest. Brace your core.
Twist the bar to unrack it and bring it over your upper chest with arms extended.
Lower the bar under control to your upper chest, allowing elbows to flare to about 45 to 70 degrees.
Press the bar back up to lockout, exhaling as you press.
Twist the bar to re-engage the hooks on your final rep. Use the safety stops for failure training.
Fixed path allows pure upper-chest focus without stabilizer demand
Safety hooks allow training to failure without a spotter
Useful for beginners learning the incline press pattern
Allows heavier loading than dumbbell incline pressing for many lifters
Easy to set up and adjust
Excellent for drop sets and high-rep hypertrophy work

description.en: The suspension trainer twist side is a rotational core move performed on TRX. The lifter grips one handle with both hands and rotates the body away from the anchor against the strap. The rotation builds strong oblique strength and rotational power.

en: Set the suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip one handle with both hands together.
Stand sideways to the anchor with feet wide.
Lean back so the body is at an angle.
Brace your core hard.
Rotate the body away from the anchor against the strap.
Squeeze the obliques hard at the end range.
Rotate back to the start with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong rotational core move
Trains the obliques
Strong TRX move
Builds rotational power
Useful core finisher
Strong functional pattern

description.en: The trap bar bent over row is a horizontal pulling exercise performed with a trap bar (hex bar) held with a neutral grip. The neutral grip is more comfortable on the wrists and shoulders than a standard barbell row, and the bar's positioning allows you to row with strict form. It is an excellent heavy back builder.

en: Stand inside a loaded trap bar with feet hip-width apart. Grip both handles with a neutral grip.
Stand up with the bar. Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is at roughly 45 degrees from horizontal.
Let the bar hang at arm’s length. Brace your core and lock in your back angle.
Row the bar up by driving your elbows back and slightly out. Keep elbows close to your body.
Pull the bar to your lower chest or upper abdomen. Squeeze your shoulder blades together.
Lower the bar under control back to arm’s length. Maintain torso angle throughout.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
The neutral grip allows heavier loading than overhand barbell rows for many lifters.
Neutral grip is comfortable on wrists and shoulders
Allows heavier loading than barbell rows for many lifters
Builds the lats, mid-traps, and rear delts
Easy to set up — no need to clean the bar from the floor
Excellent heavy back exercise
Carries over to deadlift strength

description.en: The wave walking machine is a curved manual treadmill where the lifter steps onto the curved deck and walks or runs to power the belt. The curved surface trains a natural gait and provides solid cardio. It is a low impact cardio option.

en: Step carefully onto the curved deck of the wave walker.
Hold the side rails for balance at first.
Begin stepping forward to engage the belt.
Lean slightly forward to drive the belt.
Build pace to a steady walking or running rhythm.
Pump the arms naturally as you stride.
Maintain a steady pace for the duration.
Slow down gradually and step off when finished.
Solid cardio builder
Self-powered machine
Trains a natural gait
Low impact on joints
Builds leg endurance
Useful for warm-up

description.en: The weighted lying neck side to side is a neck strengthening drill for the rotators. Lying face up with a small weight balanced on the forehead, the head rotates side to side to load the deep neck musculature.

en: Lie on the back on a bench or floor.
Hold a small weight plate flat on the forehead.
Brace the core and keep the body relaxed.
Set the chin in a neutral position.
Rotate the head slowly to one side.
Hold for a beat at the end range.
Rotate slowly back through center to the other side.
Continue alternating for the working set.
Builds the neck rotators.
Reduces neck injury risk.
Useful for combat athletes.
Trains deep cervical muscles.
Improves neck stability.
